related.why: head injury: GCS and when to scan

brief.scenario: A 47-year-old man, Declan Avery, develops an abrupt severe headache while exercising. He vomits and develops neck stiffness.
brief.task: Assess the thunderclap headache, explain the investigation pathway and immediate management after confirmation. You have 9 minutes. The examiner will give results as you ask.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: A thunderclap headache is a red flag; timing decides the investigation pathway.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Doing a lumbar puncture straight after any negative CT, or discharging after one.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: ABCDE and neurological observations, then establish the exact time of onset.

grid.label: Recognises the red flag
grid.fail: Calls it migraine and waits for the headache to settle.
grid.pass: Recognises thunderclap headache as a red flag for subarachnoid haemorrhage.
grid.high: Asks the exact time of onset and time to peak intensity, and about seizure, focal deficit and consciousness.

grid.label: Assessment and stabilisation
grid.fail: Delays assessment while waiting for imaging.
grid.pass: Performs ABCDE and repeated neurological observations, and treats pain.
grid.high: Watches for falling consciousness from rebleeding or hydrocephalus and escalates immediately.

grid.label: CT and the six-hour rule
grid.fail: Plans a lumbar puncture after every negative CT, or discharges because the CT is normal.
grid.pass: Arranges urgent non-contrast CT head; a negative CT within 6 hours, reported and documented by a radiologist, does not routinely need LP.
grid.high: Discusses alternatives with a senior clinical decision-maker; a negative early CT is not an automatic discharge instruction.

grid.label: Lumbar puncture after a later CT
grid.fail: Performs LP too early or not at all after a negative late CT.
grid.pass: Negative CT more than 6 hours after onset: considers LP, waiting at least 12 hours from onset.

grid.label: After confirmation
grid.fail: Admits under a general team without specialist discussion.
grid.pass: Arranges urgent specialist-centre discussion and CT angiography without delay.
grid.high: Considers enteral nimodipine under the specialist pathway, and does not delay transfer or treatment.

grid.label: Definitive treatment
grid.fail: Cannot say what happens to the aneurysm.
grid.pass: Explains definitive aneurysm treatment is a specialist decision.
grid.high: Names coiling and clipping as the options discussed by the specialist team.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It is probably migraine brought on by exercise. I would wait for the headache to settle.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: A CT, and then an LP straight away whatever it shows.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: The non-contrast CT report describes acute blood in the basal cisterns and subarachnoid sulci.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I would admit him to the medical ward and see how he does overnight.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It usually settles on its own.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I am concerned about subarachnoid haemorrhage. A thunderclap headache is a red-flag presentation.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would perform ABCDE and repeated neurological observations, and treat his pain.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: An urgent non-contrast CT head. If CT performed within 6 hours is negative and reported and documented by a radiologist, I would not routinely offer lumbar puncture.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What if the CT is done later?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: If CT is performed more than 6 hours after onset and is negative, lumbar puncture may be considered, at least 12 hours from symptom onset.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: The non-contrast CT report describes acute blood in the basal cisterns and subarachnoid sulci.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: That confirms subarachnoid haemorrhage. I would arrange urgent specialist-centre discussion and CT angiography without delay.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Definitive treatment of the aneurysm is a specialist decision.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Subarachnoid haemorrhage. I would ask the exact time of onset and how quickly it peaked, and about seizure, focal deficit and consciousness.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Perform ABCDE and repeated neurological observations. A fall in consciousness could mean rebleeding or hydrocephalus, so I would escalate at once.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: An urgent non-contrast CT head. If it is negative within six hours and reported and documented by a radiologist, I would not routinely do an LP; I would discuss alternatives with a senior clinical decision-maker and seek specialist advice as appropriate. A negative early CT is not an automatic discharge.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What if the CT is done later?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: After a negative CT more than six hours from onset, I would consider LP at least 12 hours from onset, with spectrophotometric CSF bilirubin/xanthochromia assessment.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The non-contrast CT report describes acute blood in the basal cisterns and subarachnoid sulci.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Perform ABCDE and repeated neurological observations; consider enteral nimodipine after confirmed SAH under the specialist pathway. Arrange urgent specialist-centre discussion and CT angiography without delay. Do not delay transfer or treatment while completing the viva.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The specialist team will decide between coiling and clipping.

failures.move: Discharges because an early CT is normal, without senior discussion.
failures.consequence: A missed haemorrhage can rebleed. This is a critical fail.

failures.move: Performs LP before 12 hours from onset.
failures.consequence: Xanthochromia may not yet be detectable.

knowledge.fact: Negative non-contrast CT within 6 hours, reported and documented by a radiologist: do not routinely offer LP.
Negative CT more than 6 hours after onset: consider LP at least 12 hours from onset, with spectrophotometry.
Confirmed SAH: urgent discussion with a specialist neurosurgical centre, CT angiography without delay, and enteral nimodipine considered under the specialist pathway.

recall.say: “Thunderclap headache is a red flag. When did it start?”
do: Confirmed: specialist centre and CT angiography

numbers.meaning: CT within this time and negative: no routine LP

recall.trap: A normal early CT as a reason to discharge.
recall.finish: Specialist-centre care: aneurysm treatment by coiling or clipping.

reveals.finding: Peak intensity within a minute, two hours ago.

reveals.finding: The non-contrast CT report describes acute blood in the basal cisterns and subarachnoid sulci.

curveballs.prompt: Is every thunderclap headache an SAH?
curveballs.safeAnswer: No, but it is a red flag requiring appropriate investigation.
